<span class="line"></span>
<span class="line"><span style="--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">public</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> Object </span><span style="--shiki-light:#6F42C1;--shiki-dark:#B392F0">pop</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">() { </span><span style="--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">return</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> elements[</span><span style="--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">--</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">size]; }</span></span></code></pre>1d:T451,<p>The <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Garbage collection" data-def="The JVM automatically finding objects that are no longer reachable and reclaiming their memory.">garbage collector</button> decides when an unreachable object is processed, and the finalizer thread may run at low priority — so a finalizer might run seconds later, much later or never before the JVM exits.</p>
<p>Resources released only by finalizers can run out long before then, like file descriptors.</p>
<p>Objects with finalizers also take much longer to allocate and reclaim, and an exception thrown inside one is swallowed silently.</p>
<p>Deterministic cleanup belongs in <code>close()</code>, called from <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="try-with-resources" data-def="&lt;code&gt;try (var in = open()) { … }&lt;/code&gt; — closes every resource declared in the parentheses automatically, in reverse order, even when an exception is thrown. Requires &lt;code&gt;AutoCloseable&lt;/code&gt;." data-book="Effective Java">try-with-resources</button>.</p>
1e:T4ae,<p>With try-finally, if the body throws and then <code>close()</code> in the <code>finally</code> block throws too, the second exception propagates and the first is discarded.</p>
<p>The first one usually explains the problem, like a read error, while the second is a consequence of it.</p>
<p><button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="try-with-resources" data-def="&lt;code&gt;try (var in = open()) { … }&lt;/code&gt; — closes every resource declared in the parentheses automatically, in reverse order, even when an exception is thrown. Requires &lt;code&gt;AutoCloseable&lt;/code&gt;." data-book="Effective Java">try-with-resources</button> keeps the original exception and attaches the <code>close</code> failure to it as a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Suppressed exception" data-def="An exception thrown while closing a resource after another exception already happened. &lt;code&gt;try&lt;/code&gt;-with-resources keeps the first and attaches the others, retrievable with &lt;code&gt;getSuppressed()&lt;/code&gt;." data-book="Effective Java">suppressed exception</button>, retrievable with <code>getSuppressed()</code>.</p>

<p>If it ignores colour when comparing with a plain <code>Point</code>, then red and blue points can both equal the same plain point, breaking <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Transitive" data-def="If &lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt; equals &lt;code&gt;y&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;y&lt;/code&gt; equals &lt;code&gt;z&lt;/code&gt;, then &lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt; equals &lt;code&gt;z&lt;/code&gt;." data-book="Effective Java">transitivity</button>.</p>
<p>There&#39;s no way to satisfy both while also keeping the <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Liskov substitution principle" data-def="Anything true of a type should be true of its subtypes — a subclass instance must work wherever the superclass is expected." data-book="Effective Java">Liskov substitution principle</button>, so favour composition: <code>ColorPoint</code> holds a <code>Point</code> and offers <code>asPoint()</code>.</p>
<p>Records and <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Value class" data-def="A class whose instances represent a value, like &lt;code&gt;Integer&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;LocalDate&lt;/code&gt;, where two instances with the same contents should be equal." data-book="Effective Java">value classes</button> sidestep the issue because they&#39;re final.</p>

<p><code>private final</code> stops <code>Period</code> from reassigning those fields, but the objects they point to are mutable, so <code>end.setTime(0)</code> changes the period&#39;s end from the outside.</p>
<p>The cure is a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Defensive copy" data-def="Copying a mutable argument when it comes in, or a mutable field when it goes out, so callers can&amp;#39;t change your object&amp;#39;s internals behind your back." data-book="Effective Java">defensive copy</button> in the constructor (and in <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Accessor method" data-def="A method that returns the value of a field — the public way in, instead of making the field itself public." data-book="Effective Java">accessors</button>), or using an <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Immutable" data-def="An object whose state can&amp;#39;t change after construction. Simple, thread-safe, freely shareable. Make fields &lt;code&gt;final&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;private&lt;/code&gt;, provide no setters, and don&amp;#39;t let the class be extended." data-book="Effective Java">immutable</button> type like <code>Instant</code> so there&#39;s nothing to copy.</p>
<p>This is why immutability must hold for the whole object graph a class exposes, not just its own fields.</p>
28:T98a,<pre class="shiki shiki-themes github-light github-dark" style="--shiki-light:#24292e;--shiki-dark:#e1e4e8;--shiki-light-bg:#fff;--shiki-dark-bg:#24292e" tabindex="0"><code><span class="line"><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">Date start </span><span style="--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583"> new</span><span style="--shiki-light:#6F42C1;--shiki-dark:#B392F0"> Date</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">(</span><span style="--shiki-light:#005CC5;--shiki-dark:#79B8FF">0</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">);</span></span>

<span class="line"><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">System.out.</span><span style="--shiki-light:#6F42C1;--shiki-dark:#B392F0">println</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">(p.</span><span style="--shiki-light:#6F42C1;--shiki-dark:#B392F0">end</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">().</span><span style="--shiki-light:#6F42C1;--shiki-dark:#B392F0">getTime</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">());</span></span></code></pre>29:T40b,<p><code>HashSet.addAll</code> happens to be implemented by calling <code>add</code> for each element — a fact documented nowhere in its contract.</p>
<p>The subclass counts 3 in its <code>addAll</code> override, then calls <code>super.addAll</code>, which calls the overridden <code>add</code> three more times, each adding 1 again.</p>
<p>The bug comes from depending on the superclass&#39;s <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Self-use" data-def="A class calling its own overridable methods. Subclasses that override them can be surprised, so it must be documented." data-book="Effective Java">self-use</button>, which can change in any release; a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Wrapper class" data-def="A class that wraps another object of the same interface and adds behavior — the Decorator pattern." data-book="Effective Java">wrapper class</button> that forwards to a private <code>Set</code> never sees these internal calls and counts exactly once.</p>

<p>A constant interface makes using some constants a permanent part of the public API, even if a later version no longer needs them.</p>
<p>The constants also leak into every subclass&#39;s namespace. Put constants in the class they belong to, an enum, or a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Noninstantiable class" data-def="A class of only static members, like &lt;code&gt;Math&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;Collections&lt;/code&gt;. <p>An identity function doesn&#39;t depend on the type at all, so one shared instance can be handed out for every <code>T</code> with an <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Unchecked warning" data-def="The compiler saying it can&amp;#39;t verify type safety at this point. Eliminate them, or prove safety and suppress with &lt;code&gt;@SuppressWarnings(&amp;quot;unchecked&amp;quot;)&lt;/code&gt; on the smallest scope." data-book="Effective Java">unchecked cast</button> that&#39;s provably safe.</p>
<p>The generic factory method hides that cast and gives each caller the type it asked for — avoiding a new object per type.</p>

<p><code>Class.cast</code> actually checks that the object is an instance of the class and throws immediately if not.</p>
<p>Since the <code>Class&lt;T&gt;</code> key carries the real type, the container can guarantee every value it returns matches what was asked for.</p>

Which one runs is decided at compile time from the static types." data-book="Effective Java">Overloading</button> is resolved at compile time from the declared types of the arguments.</p>
<p>In the loop, the variable <code>c</code> is declared as <code>Collection&lt;?&gt;</code>, so the compiler chooses <code>classify(Collection&lt;?&gt;)</code> for every call — the run-time classes <code>HashSet</code> and <code>ArrayList</code> never matter.</p>
<p><button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Overriding" data-def="A subclass redefining an inherited method. Which one runs is decided at run time from the object&amp;#39;s actual class." data-book="Effective Java">Overriding</button> is the opposite: the method runs based on the object&#39;s run-time class.</p>
<p>Code that needs run-time dispatch should use a single method with <code>instanceof</code> checks or a pattern-matching switch.</p>

<p>On <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Deserialization" data-def="Turning a byte stream back into objects. <p>No instance of the real class is ever created from raw bytes, and its fields can stay <code>final</code>.</p>
<p>Forged streams aimed at the real class are rejected, because its <code>readObject</code> simply throws.</p>

<p>Once the loop is hot and compiled, the JIT can prove the calls do nothing observable and remove them — <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Dead code elimination" data-def="The JIT removing code whose result is never used — which can make a naive benchmark measure nothing.">dead code elimination</button> — leaving an empty loop, which it may also remove.</p>
<p>The measured time then reflects nothing about <code>fib</code>. <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="JMH" data-def="The Java Microbenchmark Harness — the standard tool for writing benchmarks that the JIT can&amp;#39;t fool.">JMH</button> avoids this by consuming results in a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Blackhole" data-def="A JMH object whose &lt;code&gt;consume&lt;/code&gt; method uses a value in a way the JIT can&amp;#39;t optimize away." data-book="Java Performance"><code>Blackhole</code></button>.</p>

<span class="line"><span style="--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">long</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> elapsed </span><span style="--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">=</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> System.</span><span style="--shiki-light:#6F42C1;--shiki-dark:#B392F0">nanoTime</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">() </span><span style="--shiki-light:#D73A49;--shiki-dark:#F97583">-</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8"> start;</span></span></code></pre>cd:T42f,<p>A young collection copies the live objects out of <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Eden" data-def="The region of the young generation where new objects are allocated." data-book="Java Performance">eden</button> into a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Survivor space" data-def="One of two young-generation regions holding objects that survived a minor GC, before they&amp;#39;re promoted." data-book="Java Performance">survivor space</button>, then treats all of eden as empty.</p>
<p>It never visits the dead objects, so its cost is proportional to what survives, not to how much was allocated.</p>
<p>When most young objects are already garbage — the <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Generational hypothesis" data-def="The observation that most objects die young, which makes collecting new objects separately very efficient." data-book="Java Performance">generational hypothesis</button> — that&#39;s a tiny amount of copying for a lot of freed memory.</p>
ce:T4a0,<p>A concurrent collector does most of its marking and moving while application threads keep running, so pauses stay short.</p>
<p>That work still needs CPU, now competing with the application, and extra bookkeeping — <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Barrier" data-def="Makes a group of threads wait until all of them arrive, then releases them together. Reusable for step-by-step computations." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice">barriers</button> on reads or writes, extra memory to track objects being moved.</p>
<p>For a batch job that only cares about total runtime, a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Stop-the-world" data-def="A GC phase during which every application thread is paused." data-book="Java Performance">stop-the-world</button> <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Collector" data-def="A recipe for gathering stream elements into a result — &lt;code&gt;toList()&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;toMap(...)&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;groupingBy(...)&lt;/code&gt;." data-book="Effective Java">collector</button> like Parallel GC often finishes sooner overall.</p>
cf:T461,<p>CPU <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Cache" data-def="Keeping copies of data somewhere faster to reach, to avoid recomputing or refetching it.">caches</button> move memory in 64-byte cache lines, and a core must own a line exclusively to write to it.</p>
<p>If two counters share a line, each write by one core invalidates the other core&#39;s copy, and the line bounces back and forth.</p>
<p>The threads share no data logically, but contend physically — <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="False sharing" data-def="Threads writing to different variables that sit on the same CPU cache line, so the cores keep invalidating each other&amp;#39;s copies." data-book="Java Performance">false sharing</button>. Padding the fields onto separate lines, or <code>@Contended</code>, removes the <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Contention" data-def="Several threads wanting the same lock at once. Contended locks cost context switches and serialize work." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice">contention</button>.</p>

Casting a <code>byte</code> to <code>char</code> first <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Sign extension" data-def="Widening a signed number by copying its top (sign) bit into the new bits, so negative numbers stay negative. &lt;code&gt;(long) -1&lt;/code&gt; is all ones." data-book="Java Puzzlers">sign-extends</button> it to 16 bits set, <code>\uffff</code>.</p>
<p>Casting the <code>char</code> to <code>int</code> <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Zero extension" data-def="Widening by filling the new bits with zeros. Java does it when widening a &lt;code&gt;char&lt;/code&gt;, which is unsigned." data-book="Java Puzzlers">zero-extends</button>, because <code>char</code> is unsigned, giving 0x0000ffff, which is 65,535.</p>
<p>Whether a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Widening conversion" data-def="Converting to a type with more bits, like &lt;code&gt;int&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;long&lt;/code&gt;. The value is kept; integers are sign- or zero-extended." data-book="Java Puzzlers">widening</button> fills with ones or zeros depends on the source type being signed — an easy thing to forget in a chain of casts.</p>

<span class="line"><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">}</span></span></code></pre>150:T45b,<p>When a generic class is used as a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Raw type" data-def="A generic type used without type arguments, like &lt;code&gt;List&lt;/code&gt; instead of &lt;code&gt;List&amp;lt;String&amp;gt;&lt;/code&gt;. Exists only for compatibility; loses all type safety." data-book="Effective Java">raw type</button>, every generic type in its members is <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Erasure" data-def="Generic type arguments are checked at compile time and then removed, so at run time a &lt;code&gt;List&amp;lt;String&amp;gt;&lt;/code&gt; is just a &lt;code&gt;List&lt;/code&gt;." data-book="Effective Java">erased</button> — not just the ones involving <code>V</code>.</p>
<p>So through a raw <code>Pair</code>, <code>stringList()</code> returns a raw <code>List</code>, whose elements are <code>Object</code>.</p>
<p>The for-each loop then can&#39;t assign them to <code>String</code>. Declaring <code>p</code> as <code>Pair&lt;?&gt;</code> or <code>Pair&lt;Object&gt;</code> keeps <code>List&lt;String&gt;</code>.</p>

<span class="line"><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">}</span></span></code></pre>185:T43c,<p><code>n != n</code> reads the field twice. Without safe publication, the reader may see the reference to <code>Holder</code> before the constructor&#39;s write of <code>n</code> is visible.</p>
<p>It might read 0 on the first read and 42 on the second, and the assertion fails — a check that looks impossible.</p>
<p>The class is fine; the <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Publication" data-def="Making an object available to code outside its current scope — storing it in a shared field, returning it, passing it to another class." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice">publication</button> isn&#39;t. Making <code>n</code> final, or publishing through a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="volatile" data-def="A field modifier guaranteeing visibility — every read sees the most recent write — and ordering. Doesn&amp;#39;t make compound actions like &lt;code&gt;count++&lt;/code&gt; atomic." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice"><code>volatile</code></button> field or a lock, rules this out.</p>

<span class="line"><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">}</span></span></code></pre>18f:T434,<p><code>NumberRange</code> keeps <code>lower</code> and <code>upper</code> in two <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Atomic variable" data-def="&amp;quot;Better volatiles&amp;quot;: classes like &lt;code&gt;AtomicInteger&lt;/code&gt; with atomic compound operations such as &lt;code&gt;incrementAndGet&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;compareAndSet&lt;/code&gt;." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice"><code>AtomicInteger</code></button>s, with the <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Invariant" data-def="A condition that must always hold for an object to be valid, e.g. &lt;code&gt;lower &amp;lt;= upper&lt;/code&gt;. Variables in the same invariant must be updated atomically." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice">invariant</button> <code>lower &lt;= upper</code>. <code>setLower</code>
checks <code>i &lt;= upper.get()</code> then sets <code>lower</code>. Range is (0, 10). One thread calls <code>setLower(5)</code>, another <code>setUpper(4)</code>, at the same time. Can the range end up (5, 4)?</p>

<p>Locks on an object no other thread can reach protect nothing, so the JIT can remove them (<button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Lock elision" data-def="The JIT removing locking altogether for a lock object that it proves can&amp;#39;t be seen by other threads." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice">lock elision</button>) or merge adjacent ones into one (<button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Lock coarsening" data-def="The JIT merging adjacent &lt;code&gt;synchronized&lt;/code&gt; blocks on the same lock into one, saving repeated acquire and release." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice">lock coarsening</button>).</p>
<p>That&#39;s why uncontended synchronization is cheap in practice and rarely worth optimizing by hand.</p>

<p><code>notify</code> wakes one arbitrary waiter; if it wakes a producer when the event was &quot;item added&quot;, the producer re-waits and the consumer that should have woken stays asleep — a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Missed signal" data-def="A thread starts waiting for a condition that already became true — and its notification was sent before it waited." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice">missed signal</button> that can stall the program.</p>
<p><code>notifyAll</code> wakes everyone so the right thread is among them; explicit <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Condition" data-def="An explicit condition queue tied to a &lt;code&gt;Lock&lt;/code&gt;, created with &lt;code&gt;lock.newCondition()&lt;/code&gt;. A lock can have several, one per condition predicate." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice"><code>Condition</code></button> objects avoid the problem by giving each predicate its own queue.</p>

<span class="line"><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">        Node.class, Node.class, </span><span style="--shiki-light:#032F62;--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF">"next"</span><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">);</span></span></code></pre>23b:T47b,<p>Without synchronization, the compiler and CPU may reorder independent actions, and writes can sit in a processor&#39;s store buffer before other cores see them.</p>
<p>Thread A may effectively read <code>b</code> before its own write to <code>a</code> is visible, and thread B likewise — so both read the initial 0s.</p>
<p>Only a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Happens-before" data-def="A guarantee between two actions — if A happens-before B, B sees everything A did. Created by unlocking then locking the same lock, writing then reading a volatile, starting or joining a thread, and so on." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice">happens-before</button> relationship, created by locks, <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="volatile" data-def="A field modifier guaranteeing visibility — every read sees the most recent write — and ordering. Doesn&amp;#39;t make compound actions like &lt;code&gt;count++&lt;/code&gt; atomic." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice"><code>volatile</code></button>, thread start and join and the like, rules out such outcomes.</p>

<span class="line"><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">    }</span></span>
<span class="line"><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">}</span></span></code></pre>23e:T5cb,<p>Publishing an object means two writes: the object&#39;s fields in the constructor, and the reference into a shared field.</p>
<p>Without synchronization, nothing orders them for other threads, so a reader can see the new reference before the field writes — an object that seems to exist with default values in its fields.</p>
<p><button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Safe publication" data-def="Publishing an object so other threads see it fully constructed: via a static initializer, a &lt;code&gt;volatile&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;final&lt;/code&gt; field, a lock, or a thread-safe collection." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice">Safe publication</button>, through <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="volatile" data-def="A field modifier guaranteeing visibility — every read sees the most recent write — and ordering. Doesn&amp;#39;t make compound actions like &lt;code&gt;count++&lt;/code&gt; atomic." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice"><code>volatile</code></button>, a lock, a static initializer or a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Thread safety" data-def="A class is thread-safe if it behaves correctly when used from multiple threads, however their execution is interleaved, with no extra synchronization by the caller." data-book="Java Concurrency in Practice">thread-safe</button> collection, guarantees the reader sees the fields as constructed.</p>

<p>The two-argument version has no condition and is infinite, so it needs a <code>limit</code> or a <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Short-circuiting" data-def="Stopping as soon as the answer is known — &lt;code&gt;findFirst&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;anyMatch&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;limit&lt;/code&gt; don&amp;#39;t process the rest of the stream." data-book="Modern Java in Action">short-circuiting</button> <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Terminal operation" data-def="A stream operation, like &lt;code&gt;collect&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;forEach&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;findFirst&lt;/code&gt;, that produces a result and runs the pipeline. 264:T52c,<p><button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="ssthresh" data-def="The slow-start threshold — where TCP switches from doubling its window to growing it by one segment per round trip. Set to half the window on loss." data-book="Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach">ssthresh</button> = 12 ÷ 2 = 6, and Reno&#39;s <strong><button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Fast recovery" data-def="After fast retransmit, Reno halves the window instead of dropping to 1, since duplicate ACKs show data is still flowing." data-book="Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach">fast recovery</button></strong> sets <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Congestion window" data-def="How many unacknowledged bytes or segments TCP lets itself have in flight, based on its guess about the network&amp;#39;s capacity." data-book="Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach">cwnd</button> = ssthresh + 3 = 9, then continues in congestion

265:T40e,<p>SJF only chooses among jobs that have already arrived, and it never interrupts a running job.</p>
<p>At time 0 only A is present, so A starts and runs to completion; B and C, arriving at 4, must wait behind it.</p>
<p>The <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Convoy effect" data-def="Short jobs stuck waiting behind one long job, like cars behind a truck." data-book="Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces">convoy effect</button> returns. A <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Preemption" data-def="The OS stopping a running job to run another, without waiting for it to finish or yield." data-book="Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces">preemptive</button> policy like <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="STCF" data-def="When a new job arrives, run whichever job has the least time left, preempting if needed." data-book="Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces">STCF</button> would stop A when the shorter jobs arrive and run them first.</p>

Use <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="try-with-resources" data-def="&lt;code&gt;try (var in = open()) { … }&lt;/code&gt; — closes every resource declared in the parentheses automatically, in reverse order, even when an exception is thrown. Requires &lt;code&gt;AutoCloseable&lt;/code&gt;." data-book="Effective Java">try-with-resources</button> or <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Cleaner" data-def="The safer replacement for finalizers (&lt;code&gt;java.lang.ref.Cleaner&lt;/code&gt;): runs a cleanup action after an object becomes unreachable. Still unpredictable — only a safety net." data-book="Effective Java"><code>Cleaner</code></button> instead.</p>

<span class="line"><span style="--shiki-light:#24292E;--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8">};</span></span></code></pre>522:T461,<p>javac moves the <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Lambda" data-def="An anonymous function: parameters, an arrow and a body, like &lt;code&gt;a -&amp;gt; a.weight() &amp;gt; 150&lt;/code&gt;. It can be passed wherever a functional interface is expected." data-book="Modern Java in Action">lambda</button> body into a private synthetic method, like <code>lambda$main$0</code>.</p>
<p>At the lambda expression, it emits an <code>invokedynamic</code> whose <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Bootstrap method" data-def="The method the JVM calls the first time an &lt;code&gt;invokedynamic&lt;/code&gt; instruction runs, to decide what that call site will do." data-book="The Well-Grounded Java Developer">bootstrap method</button> is <code>LambdaMetafactory.metafactory</code>.</p>
<p>The first time it runs, the factory spins up a class implementing <code>Runnable</code> that calls the synthetic method; later executions reuse the linked call site.</p>
<p>No class file per lambda, and the JDK can change the strategy without recompiling your code.</p>
523:T414,<p><code>-Xmx</code> limits only the heap. The JVM also needs memory for metaspace, thread stacks, the <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="JIT" data-def="The JVM&amp;#39;s just-in-time compiler — turns frequently run bytecode into optimized machine code while the program runs.">JIT</button>&#39;s code <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Cache" data-def="Keeping copies of data somewhere faster to reach, to avoid recomputing or refetching it.">cache</button>, <button type="button" class="term" aria-expanded="false" data-term="Garbage collection" data-def="The JVM automatically finding objects that are no longer reachable and reclaiming their memory.">GC</button> data structures and direct buffers — often hundreds of megabytes.</p>
<p>With the heap allowed to fill the whole limit, the process eventually exceeds it, and the kernel&#39;s OOM killer terminates it with no Java stack trace.</p>
<p>Leaving headroom with <code>-XX:MaxRAMPercentage</code> avoids that.</p>
